idiom_name: object literal whose methods return the canned value
implementation_notes: In JavaScript the classic structure disappears: a stub is an object literal whose method is an arrow function returning the canned value (or throwing the canned error), passed to the SUT wherever the collaborator is injected. Nothing needs to implement an interface, because the call site only requires the property to exist, and nothing needs a framework - which is why the local idiom, not a library, is the language's default realization. jest.fn().mockReturnValue(value) and sinon.stub().returns(value) add call recording and one-time sequences (mockReturnValueOnce, onCall) and are the shortest path when the suite already uses those frameworks; the recording is what makes them spies, so reach for them when the interaction, not only the canned answer, matters. Where the collaborator is reached through a module import rather than an argument, the module itself must be replaced (jest.mock, vi.mock) instead of patching a global.
pitfalls: A jest.fn() with no configured implementation returns undefined, and code that assumes a value fails later with an unrelated error; programme the answer before handing the double over.
Spreading or destructuring the stub copies its functions, so mutating the copy in a test does not change what the SUT holds.
A collaborator imported as a module singleton bypasses injected objects entirely; stub the module (jest.mock/vi.mock) or the real implementation keeps being called.

variants.name: jest.fn()/sinon.stub() with mockReturnValue/returns
variants.implementation_notes: When the suite already runs on Jest or Sinon, the canned answer is one call: jest.fn().mockReturnValue(false), with mockReturnValueOnce for consecutive calls and mockResolvedValue/mockRejectedValue for async collaborators; Sinon writes the same as sinon.stub().returns(false) with .onCall(n) for sequences and .throws() for the error path. Both are stubs that also record, and Sinon's own documentation now recommends sinon.fake.returns() for simple cases, reserving stubs for call-specific behaviour. Configure before injection, and restore or reset in teardown (mockRestore, restore, resetAllMocks) because a leaked programmed answer is invisible until a later test fails for the wrong reason.
pitfalls: mockReturnValueOnce values are consumed in order, and calls after they run out fall back to mockReturnValue - or to undefined if none was set.
A recorded mock is also a spy: asserting on mock.calls/'toHaveBeenCalledWith' turns the double into an interaction test, which is a deliberate choice, not a stub.
Module-level stubs (jest.mock, sinon.stub(module, 'fn')) leak across tests unless restored in afterEach.
